prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "CORNING INC /NY" (ticker GLW), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "GLW", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Corning Incorporated
result.industry: Specialty glass, ceramics and optical fiber/connectivity
markets: Optical fiber, cable and connectivity for AI data centers, hyperscale and carrier networks
Cover glass for phones, tablets and wearables (Gorilla Glass)
Ceramic emissions substrates and filters for vehicles
US-made solar polysilicon, wafers and modules (Hemlock)
Life-sciences labware and pharmaceutical glass tubing

mission.plain: Corning says its job is to invent, make and sell new kinds of materials that change whole industries and make people's lives better.

about.plain: Corning is a 175-year-old company that is very good at making special glass and ceramics. It makes the thin glass threads (optical fiber) that carry internet data as light, including inside huge AI data centers. It also makes the tough glass on many phone screens, the big glass sheets inside TVs, and ceramic parts that clean car exhaust. Lately it has started making US-made materials for solar panels too.
about.customers: Big tech and telecom companies (such as Meta, Amazon, Nvidia, AT&T and Apple), TV and phone makers, carmakers, solar companies and lab scientists buy from it.
about.everyday: The scratch-resistant Gorilla Glass on many smartphones, and the fiber cables carrying your internet and AI chatbot answers, are made by Corning.

money.plain: glass fiber, cables and connectors for data centers and networks
TV and monitor glass sheets, Gorilla Glass for phones
ceramic filters that clean car exhaust, car glass
US-made polysilicon, solar wafers and panels
lab dishes and flasks, glass tubing for medicine vials
optical parts linking AI chips with light (co-packaged optics)

result.summary: Corning has a real competitive advantage built on hard-to-copy manufacturing know-how, such as its fusion-draw glass process and 50+ years of optical-fiber leadership. Customers trust it enough to sign multiyear supply and co-investment deals: Meta (up to $6B), Amazon (multibillion, June 2026), Nvidia (May 2026, $500M for warrants) and Apple ($2.5B for Kentucky cover glass). The weaker spots are cyclical, capital-heavy display and solar businesses and Chinese rivals adding capacity.

pricingPower.evidence: Corning raised display-glass prices in 2023 and again from September 2024 to offset the weak yen (DSCC estimated +3% in Q3'24 and a forecast +10% in Q4'24), while Display sales slipped 5% in 2025 as Chinese glassmakers gained share. Strong AI-driven fiber demand lifted Optical Communications sales 35% in 2025 and 32% in Q2 2026, and core gross margin rose from 38.4% to 39.6% year on year.

moats.evidence: Gorilla Glass is one of few component brands consumers know, and Corning was on Fortune's 2025 America's Most Innovative Companies list; its 175-year reputation in materials science helps win long-term deals.

Fiber, cover glass and emissions substrates must be qualified into customers' designs and plants, and recent multiyear deals with Meta, Amazon, Nvidia and Apple include customer prepayments or capital commitments (customer deposits added $880M of operating cash flow in Q2 2026).
Its products do not get more valuable as more people use them.
Corning is the largest optical-fiber and display-glass maker, with $15.6B of FY2025 sales and $1.28B of capex, but Chinese fiber and glass rivals are often lower-cost.
LCD glass has long been an oligopoly of Corning, AGC and Nippon Electric Glass because a single tank costs hundreds of millions of dollars, though Chinese Gen 8.5 capacity is now eroding this.
Its customer co-investment model (customers fund US capacity in exchange for supply) is unusual, but rivals could copy it.
Corning invented low-loss optical fiber (1970) and owns the fusion-draw process behind its display and Gorilla glass, backed by $1.11B of research, development and engineering spending in 2025.
Its large patent estate and Sullivan Park research center are valuable, but no raw material or asset is exclusive.

customers.evidence: Leading customers keep deepening long-term relationships: Apple's $2.5B Kentucky cover-glass commitment, Meta's up-to-$6B fiber agreement, Amazon's multibillion AWS deal (June 2026) and Nvidia's May 2026 partnership with $500M paid for warrants; Corning has no published NPS.

talent.evidence: Forbes listed Corning among America's Best Large Employers for 2025 (its 10th time) and it is a top materials-science employer, but it is not a top-tier employer brand like the big tech companies.

product.evidence: Corning is the #1 display-glass maker by volume and revenue (DSCC/Counterpoint, 2024), Gorilla Glass leads in smartphone cover glass, and its fiber and connectivity are the choice of hyperscalers such as Meta, AWS and Nvidia's AI build-outs.

competitors.name: Prysmian S.p.A.
competitors.note: Largest cable maker; optical fiber and cable for telecom and data centers.

competitors.name: Amphenol Corporation
competitors.note: Data-center fiber connectivity and cabling, much larger since buying CommScope's Connectivity and Cable Solutions business (closed January 2026).

competitors.note: Display glass substrates and Dragontrail cover glass; automotive glass.

competitors.name: Nippon Electric Glass Co., Ltd.
competitors.note: LCD/OLED display glass and chemically strengthened cover glass.

competitors.note: World-scale optical fiber preform, fiber and cable maker in China and abroad.

competitors.note: High-density optical fiber, cable and connectivity for AI data centers.

competitors.note: Optical fiber and cable, including OFS in the US.

competitors.name: SCHOTT AG
competitors.note: Private, foundation-owned German specialty-glass maker: cover glass, pharma tubing and vials (via listed Schott Pharma).

competitors.name: NGK Insulators
competitors.note: Ceramic substrates and particulate filters for vehicle emissions.

competitors.note: Laboratory plastics and consumables versus Corning Life Sciences.

competitors.note: Polysilicon for semiconductors and solar versus Hemlock.

competitors.note: Solar wafers and modules; Corning sells US-made wafers and panels.

threats: AI data-center spending slowing or projects being delayed, which would hit Optical Communications (44% of Q2 2026 core sales)
Chinese display-glass makers adding Gen 8.5 capacity and taking share from Corning, AGC and NEG
Chinese fiber makers (YOFC, Hengtong) and Japanese rivals (Fujikura, Sumitomo) expanding data-center fiber capacity
Co-packaged optics or other new interconnects changing how much fiber and which connectors AI clusters need
Solar business depends on US trade policy and incentives; it lost $7M in Q2 2026 after extended wafer-plant maintenance
Customer concentration in a few hyperscalers and Apple, plus yen exposure in Display
Dilution from the $2B at-the-market equity program announced in September 2026 and Nvidia warrants for up to 15M shares at $180

ceo.name: Wendell P. Weeks
ceo.background: Lehigh University graduate, Harvard MBA (Baker Scholar); joined Corning's finance group in 1983 and ran its optical-fiber business; chairman since 2007, also on Amazon's board

c1.evidence: Corning leads optical fiber and connectivity for AI data centers, a fast-growing market where its Optical Communications sales rose 35% in 2025 and 32% in Q2 2026, but much of the company (display, auto, life sciences) is in mature industries.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Corning for materials-science innovation and dependable scale (it invented low-loss fiber and fusion-draw glass), and that know-how, plus multiyear deals with Meta, Amazon, Nvidia and Apple, is hard to copy and likely to last.

c3.evidence: Many consumers recognise Gorilla Glass and Pyrex's heritage, and Corning is the default leader in display glass and fiber, but the Corning name itself is far less known than Google or NVIDIA.

c4.evidence: Management stresses 'invent, make and sell' and inventing category-defining products, which matters for AI networks and US manufacturing, but Corning does not publish a widely quoted, inspiring mission statement.

c6.evidence: “Gorilla Glass, fiber optics, innovative, old-line glassmaker”: the impression is mostly positive, of a durable science-led manufacturer, though investors also see it as cyclical.

c7.evidence: AI data-center fiber demand is a large, growing secular trend; Corning targets a $30B annualized sales run rate by end-2028 and $40B by end-2030, up from $16.4B core sales in 2025.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into US solar polysilicon, wafers and modules (Solar sales +90% in Q2 2026) and launched a photonics market-access platform in May 2026 that management thinks could be a $10B revenue stream by 2030.

m1.evidence: Weeks foresaw the AI fiber build-out and set the Springboard plan in late 2023, hitting its 20% core operating-margin goal a year early.

m2.evidence: Weeks has spent 43 years at Corning and 21 as CEO with a long-term, R&D-heavy approach, but he is a professional manager, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way on whether Weeks leads in a servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: Corning keeps a strong inventing culture, spending $1.11B on RD&E in 2025, and has gone from Gorilla Glass (2007) to new photonics and AI-connectivity products.

m6.evidence: Weeks is closely involved in strategy and ran the optical-fiber business, but his training is in finance and business (Harvard MBA), not engineering.

m7.evidence: Weeks talks about US manufacturing jobs (for example 1,000 new jobs in the Amazon deal and over 3,000 with Nvidia), but there is little public evidence of a mission beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Wendell Weeks at a top university could be confirmed.

m8b.evidence: Weeks has a low-key, conventional corporate profile, not a celebrity-founder personality.

m9.evidence: Under Weeks, revenue grew from $13.1B in 2024 to $15.6B in 2025 and core EPS rose 29% to $2.52, with core EPS up 30% in Q2 2026, though growth over 2021-2024 was flat.

m10.evidence: Corning is not known for frugality; it is capital-intensive ($1.28B of capex in 2025) and spends heavily on research.

c10.evidence: Its fiber carries much of the world's internet and data traffic, and its glass is in many of the world's phones and TVs, so its products touch a very large number of people.

p2.evidence: Ultra-pure fiber, ultra-flat display glass and damage-resistant cover glass need decades of process know-how, and they are vital to communications and AI.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 2021, 2022, 2024 and 2025 (to $15,629M) but fell 11% in 2023 to $12,588M.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin moved from 31.2% (2020) to 36.0% (2025) and operating margin from 4.5% to 14.6%, but both peaked in 2021 (36.0%, 15.0%) and dipped in 2022-2024.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive at $12.56B, but total debt of $8.42B is over three times cash of $2.50B (June 2026), about 3.5 times trailing free cash flow of $2.40B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $509M (2020) to $2,279M (2025), but operating cash flow was $2,180M in 2020, $3,412M in 2021 and $2,695M in 2025, so it has not risen steadily.

v1.evidence: Corning fiber and Gorilla Glass are widely seen as the quality leaders, but rivals such as Prysmian, Fujikura, AGC and NEG make close substitutes, so it is not an NVIDIA-like clear winner.

v2.evidence: Forbes named Corning one of America's Best Large Employers for 2025 (its 10th time), but it does not appear near the top of the best-known employer rankings.

c5.evidence: If Corning vanished, hyperscalers building AI data centers, phone makers and TV-panel makers would face shortages of fiber and specialty glass for years.
